name: Nose bone massaging / nasal bone pushing

lead: Nose bone massaging is a bonehack in which people press or massage the nose, usually the bridge, hoping to narrow or reshape it.
No clinical study has tested this on healthy noses; the medical literature on nasal bones is about fractures and surgery.

paras: Proponents' idea is that repeated pressure moves the nasal bones or the structures around them. Anatomy sources describe a bone-and-cartilage framework that surgeons reshape operatively, and none has examined massage.
No studies have measured the effects of self-applied pressure on the nose. Trauma reviews note that injured noses need assessment for septal hematoma, which requires emergency treatment.

web.title: Nose bone massaging / nasal bone pushing — Grokipedia

lead: Nose bone massaging, or nasal bone pushing, is a bonehacking practice in which a person presses or massages the nose, usually the bridge, in the belief that this can narrow it or change its shape without surgery.

The nasal bones are two small paired bones forming the bridge of the upper third of the nose, joined at the midline and attached to the frontal bone and maxilla [1]. Medical literature on the nasal bones deals almost entirely with fractures and their reduction or surgical correction [2][3]. No published study that the wiki has located has tested whether pressing or massaging the nose reshapes it in healthy people.

paras: Shape and size of the nasal bones vary widely between individuals [1]. The visible form of the nose also depends on the cartilage framework below the bones, including the paired upper lateral cartilages, the lower lateral cartilages that form the tip and the septum, which surgeons reshape in rhinoplasty [4].

No studies found on massage or pressure as a method of reshaping the uninjured nose. Clinical research on the nasal bones concerns trauma. Isolated nasal fractures are described as the most common injury of the central midface [2], and reviews note that management of fractures varies widely between surgeons [3]. A review in the German literature states that closed reduction can be offered for misalignment once swelling has subsided, and that rhinoplasty or septal reconstruction is considered no earlier than 6 to 12 months after the injury if results are insufficient [2]. These sources concern injured noses, not routine massage.

Trauma reviews emphasize that injury to the nose requires exclusion of septal hematoma or abscess, which need emergency surgical treatment [2]. These findings relate to injury, and no studies have measured the effects of self-applied pressure on the nose.
